title: Output-sensitive sparse factorization over finite fields from dense factorization
assumptions: p is a promised prime given in binary; L = ceil(log2(p)).
K = F_p[T]/(h), with an explicit monic irreducible h of degree m at least 1, using coefficient coordinates over F_p.
The nonzero input is sparse, with t nonzero terms and distinct nonnegative binary exponents; N is its degree and b = max(1, ceil(log2(N+1))).
Output is all distinct monic irreducible factors in dense representation, with binary positive multiplicities and the leading coefficient; D is the sum of distinct factor degrees.
The dense or prime-field factorization subroutine is a complete exact oracle for the reduction; its unconditional polynomial implementation is a separate dependency.
The prescribed construction degree d is a numeric output-size parameter; polynomial dependence on log(d) is not claimed.

exact_checked_claims.statement: Theorem 1: deterministic sparse complete factorization reduces to at most 2b dense factorization calls, each of degree at most (b+1)D, aggregate degree O(b^2 D), with polynomial nonoracle bit cost in t,b,D,m,L.

Exact known-factor valuation via base-p residue recursion and an invertible binomial evaluation matrix; the least residue of multiplicity is at most t-1. Integer exponents are retained, including at roots of unity.

The reduced denominator of U-prime/U is exactly the product of factors whose multiplicity is nonzero modulo p. Doubling Padé reconstruction is accepted only after the exact identity U-prime Q = U A, rather than a finite series prefix.

Signed Cartier descent preserves U/V as a polynomial, keeps the sparse numerator support at most t, shrinks numerator degree by a factor p, keeps the new denominator degree at most the old denominator degree plus D, and cancels foreign factors through the signed multiplicity ledger.

Both section operands use inverse coefficient Frobenius in extension fields. The new numerator and denominator correctly represent the quotient of p-th roots; replacing coefficients unchanged is generally invalid.

Theorem 2: complete dense factorization over represented K reduces to at most mn prime-field calls of degrees at most n and aggregate degree at most mn^2 by trace coordinates; the direct F_p-linear fixed-algebra variant uses at most n calls with aggregate degree at most n^2.

Prescribed-degree irreducible construction follows at oracle level through prime-field construction and extension-field factorization, with the stated explicit field model and numeric output degree. Shoup reduction statements and exceptional cases were checked in the original source.

Coordinate sizes, binary exponent operations, inverse Frobenius, Gaussian elimination dimensions, sparse-dense products and signed multiplicity growth give polynomial bit overhead. A conservative substitution supports the displayed loose exponent bound.
limitations: No formal instruction-level complexity certificate was built.

exact_checked_claims.statement: Corollary 3 follows if the pinned upstream deterministic polynomial-time prime-field factorization theorem is valid. Its statement matches the required complete factorization, binary prime and bit-cost interface.

The upstream factorization manuscript Section 11 supplies a polynomial auxiliary-prime bound conditional on the exact general-cyclotomic finite-order Hecke zero-free theorem in its pinned primitive-root manuscript.
limitations: This check does not certify either full upstream proof.

strongest_verified_result: The complete sparse reduction and represented-field-to-prime-field reductions are independently supported as deterministic oracle implications in their stated dense-distinct-factor output model, including arbitrary binary multiplicities and extension-field Frobenius.
exact_remaining_gap: Full correctness of the pinned 48-page deterministic prime-field factorization algorithm and the pinned 92-page general-cyclotomic Hecke zero-free input has not been independently reconstructed. Therefore the unconditional polynomial-time corollary is not certified by this review. This is an unresolved dependency and coverage limitation, not an identified counterexample or demonstrated defect.
